extracted.intended_audience: novelists, writers of long-form fiction, and students of fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating expansive, multi-threaded novels (epics) — focusing on unity of subject and form, representation of time and space, point of view, and management of many characters and themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject must be a single, expressible idea
rubrics_metrics.description: The novel must have a subject that can be put into a phrase; 'If it cannot be put into a phrase it is no subject for a novel.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Until the subject is known and expressible, the form cannot be determined. The subject — simple or complex — supplies the support on which the novel's form is built. If a novelist cannot state the intention succinctly, the book will lack a coherent form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form must coincide with the subject
rubrics_metrics.description: The best form is that which makes the most of its subject — a book in which 'the matter is all used up in the form, in which the form expresses all the matter.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the book so that form and matter are indistinguishable. Where they conflict, material will be superfluous or wanting; the reader senses loss of potential or surplus. Use the form to express every aspect of the chosen subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of design / avoid writing two novels at once
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not mix two independent designs or master-motives in the same book; a book must have a centre. Example anti-pattern: War and Peace's simultaneous treatment of 'the march of generations' and the 'drama of war and peace', producing a confusion of two designs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether the novel's centre is one grand subject or another, and subordinate all material to that centre. If two large themes are intended, either find a principled way to unite them or treat them in separate works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of material; avoid wasteful importation
rubrics_metrics.description: A novel should not be wasteful of its subject; importation of irrelevant storyline or material damages the story's power. Tolstoy is criticized for importing 'another and an irrelevant story' into his principal narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prune or relocate material that does not serve the main subject. Superfluous digressions or added cycles dilute impact and leave the primary story incomplete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion and overall design (whole beyond parts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Good parts do not guarantee a good whole: scenes and episodes may be lucid and shapely while the overall novel lacks proportion or design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a long work, check the relation of parts to overall shape. Ensure episodes are grouped and arranged to create proportion — not merely a succession of excellent scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistent point of view / coherent narrative method
rubrics_metrics.description: The author must maintain a coherent method of presentation; inconsistent alternation between an omniscient authorial narrator and character-centred perspective undermines unity ('the predominant point of view is simply his own' vs scenes where 'Tolstoy is effaced').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose and sustain a method (authorial commentary, interior focalisation through characters, or consistent onlooker) except where deliberate shifts serve a principled artistic purpose. Random shifts make the book feel disunited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid authorial digression and 'pamphleteering'
rubrics_metrics.description: Long chapters of commentary or polemic interrupt the novelistic action and are damaging ('interminable chapters of comment and explanation, chapters in the manner of a controversial pamphlet').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep theoretical or polemical material out of the narrative flow; if argument is necessary, either integrate it seamlessly into character experience or place it in a separate essay. Readers often skip overtly didactic interruptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of time: show passage through form, not labels
rubrics_metrics.description: The passage of time must be represented by the build and shape of the book, not by mere announcements that 'years have fled'; both the continuous lapse and the cyclic rise-and-fall must be made perceptible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make time visible in changes to characters' faces, habits, circumstances, and in the patterning of events. Structure the narrative so the reader feels slow accrual and also the arc (rise and decline) of the chosen period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate scale and length relative to theme
rubrics_metrics.description: The size of the book must suit the scale of the theme; a vast theme requires generous room, and a theme treated fragmentarily will feel incomplete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure you provide the requisite space to develop the theme fully. If a theme demands an epic treatment (e.g., national saga), commit to it or else limit the novel's scope to what can be coherently addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of setting and historical background should support, not dominate
rubrics_metrics.description: Background (e.g., war) should serve as foil or occasion that illuminates the main human drama, not displace or dominate it ('the historic scene is used as a foil and a background' or becomes the centre to the detriment of personal drama).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether historical events are backdrop or principal subject. Frame battle/historical scenes through the lives and perceptions of central characters if the human story is primary; otherwise structure the work as a historical epic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice and handling of observers/onlookers for indirectness
rubrics_metrics.description: Using an onlooker (a minor character, an officer, a small child) can increase indirectness and effect; but choosing observers 'at random' and following no consistent method weakens the unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select vantage points deliberately: whose consciousness will mediate big events? Use consistent criteria for whose perception shapes each scene, and avoid arbitrary switches that confuse focalisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Population and representation: populate for universality
rubrics_metrics.description: A subject like the march of generations requires a large, various population so central figures appear representative rather than exceptional; the world must open beyond the few protagonists ('a receding crowd...swelling the impression of swarming life').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce sufficient households, names, and connections to make central characters feel embedded in a larger life. But ensure these additional figures serve the representative purpose rather than merely cluttering the page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create a convincing sense of space and horizon when required
rubrics_metrics.description: For some fables, an open, limitless horizon (space, daylight) is essential to effect; for others a closed, night-like curtain suits the interior drama (contrast Tolstoy's open day with Dostoevsky's enclosing darkness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether your story requires an expansive world or an enclosed theatre of consciousness, and deploy description, scene-setting, and movement to create that chosen horizon faithfully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance panorama and detail; command both masses and small scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: A great novel can combine panoramic reach (armies, nations) with exquisite treatment of single episodes and fine shades of character; mastery lies in handling both 'spaces and masses' and 'the single episode.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternate and integrate large-scale canvases with intimate scenes so the grand sweep amplifies human particulars and particulars illuminate the sweep. Avoid privileging one at the complete expense of the other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and steadiness of character handling across many figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Even in crowded novels the author must never lose hold of character; there should be no faltering among the many men and women, no hesitating intention in scenes and events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain distinctive, stable characterisation so readers can follow dozens of figures; use recurring motifs, households, and relational anchors to keep identities clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid casual or fragmentary transitions between themes
rubrics_metrics.description: Shifts from one dominant narrative line to another should not occur casually (sometimes 'in the middle of a page'); random sprinkling of alternations undermines cohesion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signal transitions convincingly or structure chapter and section breaks so that changes in dominant theme feel intentional and legible, not capricious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form should make apparent the reason for telling the story
rubrics_metrics.description: The shape of the story must give the reason for telling it — the form must reflect the author's purpose in chronicling the facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging or designing a novel, ask what the author wants the reader to take away and ensure structural choices (order, emphasis, focalisation) lead to that effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader participation: deliberate, critical reading recreates and sustains a work
rubrics_metrics.description: A deliberately recreated reading — an uncritical, casual reading would let the book 'perish' — prolongs the book's effect; the reader's active re-creation helps the work endure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write so the reader can re-create scenes and fill in gaps; encourage re-readings by leaving material that rewards deliberate, critical attention rather than only immediate impression.
